question: to the Commission Moritz Körner (Renew) Subject:

In Germany, around 9.38 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity from renewable sources had to be curtailed due to redispatching interventions in 2025. Operators of the plants concerned received approximately EUR 434.5 million in financial compensation as a result. 1.
What was the scale and cost of renewable energy curtailment in the other Member States? The Commission is asked to provide data on all Member States for 2025.
How does the Commission assess the scale of renewable energy curtailment and the associated compensation payments in Germany?

In the Commission’s view, how is a system under which operators are also compensated for curtailed electricity and electricity not fed into the grid expected to create effective incentives to develop grid infrastructure as needed?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.10.2026) The Commission agrees it is important to monitor renewable energy sources (RES) curtailment levels. There is currently no consistent EU-wide definition of curtailment, making it difficult to measure in a consistent manner. Realised curtailment levels are heterogeneously reported by national system operators with varying methodologies and definitions. It is estimated that in 2024 the cost of curtailment amounted to over EUR 6 bn in six countries1 and over 10 TWh of electricity from RES could not be used in the EU due to grid congestion and insufficient availability of cross-border capacity2. Whilst a certain level of curtailment may help manage overall system costs, high levels of curtailment can be an indicator of system failures limiting the integration of renewable electricity. Developing a common EU wide definition of RES curtailment could increase transparency, support a more coherent approach to curtailment monitoring, and improve locational investment signals for grid development, flexibility and RES generation. The power sector in the EU is unbundled: power plant operators receive redispatching compensation while grid expansion is carried out by system operators. Effective incentives for grid development are provided through the regulatory framework; including grid planning obligations, cost-recovery rules, performance-based regulation and public oversight. The Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) also funds cross-border energy infrastructure, and the Commission has proposed a five-fold increase (EUR 29.9 bn) in its budget for CEF-Energy in the next Multiannual Financial Framework. Finally, support mechanisms must be welldesigned to avoid grid congestion curtailment being compensated for through redispatching3.
1 Costs refer to country-specific curtailment payments, re-dispatch and/or counter-trading costs. Combined
